\centerline{\titlefont Parametrization of Pythagorean triples}
\smallskip
\centerline{\titlefont by a single triple of polynomials}
\bigskip\medskip

\centerline{\authorfont Sophie Frisch {\tenrm and} Leonid Vaserstein}
\footnote{\vphantom{*}}
{2000 Math.~Subj.~Classification: primary 11D09, secondary 11D85, 11C08, 13F20.}
\bigskip\bigskip\medskip
 

{\bf Abstract.} 
It is well known that Pythagorean triples can be parametrized by two
triples of polynomials with integer coefficients. We show that no
single triple of polynomials with integer coefficients in any number
of variables is sufficient, but that there exists a parametrization 
of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of integer-valued polynomials.
%MSC 2000: primary 11D09, secondary 11C08, 13F20.
\bigskip\medskip

The second author has recently studied polynomial parametrizations
of solutions of Diophantine equations \cite{Vas--PPDE}, and the 
first author has wondered if it were possible in some cases to
parametrize by a $k$-tuple of integer-valued polynomials a 
solution set that is not parametrizable by a $k$-tuple of 
polynomials with integer coefficients \cite{Fri--RPP}.
\Pt s provide an example that this is indeed so.

We call a triple of integers $(x,y,z)\in\intz^3$ satisfying
$$ x^2+y^2=z^2$$
a \Pt, and, if $x,y,z>0$, a positive \Pt.
%If in addition $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$, we say that $(x,y,z)$ is a primitive \Pt.

It is well known that every \Pt\ is either of the form 
$$\left(c(a^2-b^2),\; 2cab,\; c(a^2+b^2)\right)$$
or of the form
$$\left(2cab,\; c(a^2-b^2),\; c(a^2+b^2)\right)$$
with $a,b,c\in\intz$, see for instance~\cite{HlaSch79ZT}.

To make precise our usage of the term polynomial parametrization,
consider a set $S\subseteq \intz^k$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ be a $k$-tuple
of polynomials either in the ring of polynomials with integer 
coefficients in $n$ variables, $\intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, or in
$$\Int(\intz^n)=\{f\in\ratq[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\mid
\forall a\in \intz^n\; f(a)\in\intz\},$$
the ring of integer-valued polynomials in $n$ variables,
% cf. \cite{CaCh97ivp}, 
for some $n$. In either case $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$
defines a function $F\colon \intz^n\rightarrow \intz^k$.
If $S$ is the image of this function, $S=F(\intz^n)$,
we say that $(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$ parametrizes $S$. We call this a 
parametrization of $S$ by a single $k$-tuple of polynomials.

If $S\subseteq \intz^k$ is the union of the images of finitely many
$k$-tuples of polynomials $F_i=(f_{i1},\ldots,f_{ik})$, 
$S=\bigcup_{i=1}^m F_i(\intz^n)$, we call this a parametrization
of $S$ by a finite number of $k$-tuples of polynomials, and we
distinguish between parametrizations by polynomials with integer
coefficients, meaning $F_i\in (\intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n])^k$ for
all $i$, and by integer-valued polynomials, meaning 
$F_i\in (\Int(\intz^n))^k$.
Unless explicitly specified otherwise, we are using integer parameters,
that is, we let all variables of all polynomials range through the
integers.

We will give a parametrization of the set of \Pt s by a single
triple of integer-valued polynomials in $4$ variables, that is, by 
$(f_1,f_2,f_3)$ with $f_i\in \ratq[x,y,z,w]$ such that
$f_i(x,y,z,w)\in\intz$ whenever $x,y,z,w\in\intz$.
First we will show that it is not possible to parametrize \Pt s 
by a single triple of polynomials with integer coefficients in
any number of variables.

Note, however, that every set of $k$-tuples of integers that is
parametrizable by a single $k$-tuple of integer-valued polynomials 
is parametrizable by a finite number of $k$-tuples of polynomials
with integer coefficients \cite{Fri--RPP}.

\profess{Remark.} 
There do not exist $f,g,h\in \intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ for any $n$
such that $(f,g,h)$ parametrizes the set of \Pt s.
\endprofess

\proof
Suppose $(f,g,h)$ parametrizes the \Pt s. As $\intz[\x]$ is a unique
factorization domain, there exists $d=\gcd(g,h)$ (unique up to sign),
which also divides $f$, since $f^2+g^2=h^2$. 
Let $\varphi=f/d$, $\psi=g/d$ and $\theta=h/d$. 

Then $$\varphi^2= \theta^2 - \psi^2=(\theta+\psi)(\theta-\psi)$$
and $\gcd((\theta+\psi), (\theta-\psi))$ is either $1$ or $2$, but
it can't be $2$, because there exist \Pt s with odd first coordinate
such as $(3,4,5)$. Since $(\theta+\psi)$ and $(\theta-\psi)$ are
co-prime and their product is a square, $(\theta+\psi)$ and
$(\theta-\psi)$ are either both squares, or both $(-1)$ times a square,
and we can get rid of the latter alternative by retro-actively changing
the sign of the polynomial $d$, if necessary.

So there exist polynomials $s$ and $t$ with $(\theta+\psi)=s^2$
and $(\theta-\psi)=t^2$, and therefore 
$$\theta= {s^2+t^2\over 2}\quad \hbox{\rm and}\quad
\psi = {s^2-t^2\over 2}.$$

Since $s^2-t^2 =(s+t)(s-t)$ is divisible by $2$, it is actually 
divisible by $4$, so that $\psi $ is divisible by $2$, which
contradicts the existence of \Pt s with odd second coordinate
such as $(4,3,5)$.
\endproof

%Let $$\Int(\intz^n)=\{f\in\ratq[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\mid
%\forall {\underline a}\in \intz^n\; f({\underline a})\in\intz\},$$
%the ring of integer-valued polynomials in $n$ variables,
%cf. \cite{CaCh97ivp}.
%
In a way, it was the unique factorization property of $\intz[\x]$
that prevented us from finding a triple of polynomials in $\intz[\x]$
parametrizing \Pt s. Before we construct a parametrization
of \Pt s by a triple of integer-valued polynomials, we remark in
passing that $\Int(\intz^n)$ does not enjoy unique factorization
into irreducibles. An example of non-unique factorization into 
irreducibles in $\Int(\intz)$ is given by 
$$x(x-1)\ldots(x-k+1)=k! {x\choose k}.$$
The lefthand side is a product of $k$ irreducibles, while the 
righthand side, after factorization of $k!$ in $\intz$, becomes a
product of far more irreducibles (for large $k$).
(See \cite{CaCh97ivp} for integer-valued polynomials in general,
and \cite{AnCaChSm95FP,CahCha95El,ChaMcC05IPFE} for factorization
properties.)

\profess{Theorem.}
There exist $f,g,h\in \Int(\intz^4)$ such that $(f,g,h)$
parametrizes the set of \Pt s (as the variables range through $\intz$)
namely,
$$\displaylines{
\Biggl( {(2x-xw)((y+zw)^2-(z-yw)^2)\over 2},\hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl)} (2x-xw)(y+zw)(z-yw), \hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl(} {(2x-xw)((y+zw)^2+(z-yw)^2)\over 2}\Biggr).\cr
}$$
\endprofess

\proof
Every \Pt\ $(x,y,z)$ with $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is either of the
form
$$T_1(a,b)=(a^2-b^2,\; 2ab,\; a^2+b^2),$$
or of the form
$$T_2(a,b)=(2ab,\; a^2-b^2,\; a^2+b^2),$$
with $a,b\in \intz$.
Since $$ 2\, T_2(a,b) = T_1(a+b,\> a-b),$$ every \Pt\ with
$\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is of
the form $c\, T_1(a,b)/2$ with $c\in\{1,2\}$ and $a,b\in \intz$.
Let 
$$T(a,b,c)=
\left({c(a^2-b^2)\over 2},\; cab,\; {c(a^2+b^2)\over 2}\right).$$
Then every \Pt\ is of the form $T(a,b,c)$ with 
$a,b,c\in\intz$. Also, every triple $T(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c\in\intz$
is a rational solution of $x^2+y^2=z^2$.

So, the set of \Pt s is precisely the set of integer triples in
the range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$.

Now $T(a,b,c)\in \intz^3$ if and only if $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or
$a\congr b$ mod $2$.
Triples $(a,b,c)\in\intz^3$ satisfying this condition can be 
parametrized by (for instance) 
$$(y+zw,\; z-yw,\; 2x-xw).$$ 
Indeed, if $w$ is even then $c\congr 0$ mod $2$, if $w$ is odd then 
$a\congr b$ mod $2$, and all $(a,b,c)$ satisfying either congruence
actually occur for some $(x,y,z,w)\in\intz^4$, as can be seen by
setting $w=0$ or $w=1$.

Therefore, substituting $y+zw$ for $a$, $z-yw$ for $b$,
and $2x-xw$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ yields a parametrization of
the set of \Pt s by a triple of integer-valued polynomials.
\endproof

\profess{Remark.}
The set of positive \Pt s is parametrized by
$$\displaylines{
\Biggl( {(x+(1-w)^2x)((y+(1+w)z)^2-y^2)\over 2} \vphantom{\Biggr)},\hfill\cr
\hfill\vphantom{\Biggl({1\over f}} (x+(1-w)^2x)(y+(1+w)z)y, \hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl(} {(x+(1-w)^2x)((y+(1+w)z)^2+y^2)\over 2}\Biggr).\cr
}$$
where $x,y,z$ range through the positive integers and $w$ through the
non-negative integers. From this formula, a parametrization of positive
\Pt s with integer parameters can be obtained (using the 4-square theorem)
by replacing $w$ by $w_1^2+w_2^2+w_3^2+w_4^2$ and $x,\,y,\,z$ by
$x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2+x_4^2+1$, $y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2+y_4^2+1$, 
and $z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2+z_4^2+1$, respectively.
\endprofess

\proof
As in the proof of the theorem above, the positive \Pt s are
precisely the triples with positive integer coordinates in the
range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$.
Now $T(a,b,c)$ is a positive triple if and only if $a,b,c$ are
positive integers with $a> b$ and either $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or
$a\congr b$ mod $2$.
Such triples $(a,b,c)$ are parametrized by (for instance)
$$(y+(1+w)z,\> y,\> x+(1-w)^2x)$$
with $x,y,z>0$ and $w\ge 0$. Therefore substituting $y+(1+w)z$ for
$a$, $y$ for $b$ and $x+(1-w)^2x$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ gives a
parametrization of positive \Pt s where $w$ ranges through 
non-negative integers and $x,y,z$ through positive integers.
The 4-square theorem allows us to convert this to a parametrization
with 16 integer parameters.
\endproof

```lean
import Mathlib

open scoped BigOperators

/-! # Parametrization of Pythagorean Triples by Polynomials

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

end Definitions

section Constructions

/-- The first component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def f_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w
  (c * (u^2 - v^2)) / 2

/-- The second component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def g_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w
  c * u * v

/-- The third component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def h_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w
  (c * (u^2 + v^2)) / 2

/-- The explicit parametrization as a triple (Theorem, line 194). -/
def T_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ × ℤ × ℤ := (f_param a, g_param a, h_param a)

/-- The first component of the positive triples parametrization (Remark, line 240). -/
def f_pos_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := x + (1 - w)^2 * x
  let u := y + (1 + w) * z
  (c * (u^2 - y^2)) / 2

/-- The second component of the positive triples parametrization (Remark, line 240). -/

  let u := y + (1 + w) * z

  let w := a 3
  let c := x + (1 - w)^2 * x
  let u := y + (1 + w) * z

/-!
### Remark (line 143): Impossibility with integer coefficient polynomials

**Source proof:** Suppose (f,g,h) parametrizes the PTs. As ℤ[x] is a UFD,
there exists d = gcd(g,h) which also divides f since f²+g²=h². Let φ=f/d,
ψ=g/d, θ=h/d. Then φ² = (θ+ψ)(θ-ψ). The gcd of (θ+ψ) and (θ-ψ) is either 1
or 2, but not 2 because there exist PTs with odd first coordinate. Since they
are coprime and their product is a square, each is a square (up to sign).
Changing the sign of d if needed, we get θ+ψ = s² and θ-ψ = t². Then
θ = (s²+t²)/2 and ψ = (s²-t²)/2. Since s²-t² is divisible by 4, ψ is
divisible by 2, contradicting the existence of PTs with odd second coordinate.
-/

/-- There do not exist polynomials f,g,h ∈ ℤ[x₁,...,xₙ] for any n that parametrize
all Pythagorean triples. -/
theorem no_integer_poly_parametrization :
    ¬∃ (n : ℕ) (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ),
      IsPolyParametrization pythagoreanTriples f g h := by
  sorry

/-!
### Theorem (line 194): Existence with integer-valued polynomials

**Source proof:** Every primitive PT is T₁(a,b) or T₂(a,b). Since
2·T₂(a,b) = T₁(a+b,a-b), every primitive PT is c·T₁(a,b)/2 with c∈{1,2}.

some a,b,c ∈ ℤ. Also T(a,b,c) ∈ ℤ³ iff c ≡ 0 (mod 2) or a ≡ b (mod 2).

/-! # Parametrization of Pythagorean Triples by Polynomials

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

end Definitions

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}

  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

/-! # Parametrization of Pythagorean Triples by Polynomials

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/]

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

end Definitions

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/

  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

\centerline{\authorfont Sophie Frisch {\tenrm and} Leonid Vaserstein}
\footnote{\vphantom{*}}

\bigskip\bigskip\medskip
 

{\bf Abstract.} 
It is well known that Pythagorean triples can be parametrized by two
triples of polynomials with integer coefficients. We show that no
single triple of polynomials with integer coefficients in any number
of variables is sufficient, but that there exists a parametrization 
of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of integer-valued polynomials.
%MSC 2000: primary 11D09, secondary 11C08, 13F20.
\bigskip\medskip

The second author has recently studied polynomial parametrizations
of solutions of Diophantine equations \cite{Vas--PPDE}, and the 
first author has wondered if it were possible in some cases to
parametrize by a $k$-tuple of integer-valued polynomials a 
solution set that is not parametrizable by a $k$-tuple of 
polynomials with integer coefficients \cite{Fri--RPP}.
\Pt s provide an example that this is indeed so.

We call a triple of integers $(x,y,z)\in\intz^3$ satisfying
$$ x^2+y^2=z^2$$
a \Pt, and, if $x,y,z>0$, a positive \Pt.
%If in addition $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$, we say that $(x,y,z)$ is a primitive \Pt.

It is well known that every \Pt\ is either of the form 
$$\left(c(a^2-b^2),\; 2cab,\; c(a^2+b^2)\right)$$
or of the form
$$\left(2cab,\; c(a^2-b^2),\; c(a^2+b^2)\right)$$
with $a,b,c\in\intz$, see for instance~\cite{HlaSch79ZT}.

To make precise our usage of the term polynomial parametrization,
consider a set $S\subseteq \intz^k$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ be a $k$-tuple
of polynomials either in the ring of polynomials with integer 
coefficients in $n$ variables, $\intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, or in
$$\Int(\intz^n)=\{f\in\ratq[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\mid
\forall a\in \intz^n\; f(a)\in\intz\},$$
the ring of integer-valued polynomials in $n$ variables,
% cf. \cite{CaCh97ivp}, 
for some $n$. In either case $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$
defines a function $F\colon \intz^n\rightarrow \intz^k$.
If $S$ is the image of this function, $S=F(\intz^n)$,
we say that $(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$ parametrizes $S$. We call this a 
parametrization of $S$ by a single $k$-tuple of polynomials.

If $S\subseteq \intz^k$ is the union of the images of finitely many
$k$-tuples of polynomials $F_i=(f_{i1},\ldots,f_{ik})$, 
$S=\bigcup_{i=1}^m F_i(\intz^n)$, we call this a parametrization
of $S$ by a finite number of $k$-tuples of polynomials, and we
distinguish between parametrizations by polynomials with integer
coefficients, meaning $F_i\in (\intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n])^k$ for
all $i$, and by integer-valued polynomials, meaning 
$F_i\in (\Int(\intz^n))^k$.
Unless explicitly specified otherwise, we are using integer parameters,
that is, we let all variables of all polynomials range through the
integers.

We will give a parametrization of the set of \Pt s by a single
triple of integer-valued polynomials in $4$ variables, that is, by 
$(f_1,f_2,f_3)$ with $f_i\in \ratq[x,y,z,w]$ such that
$f_i(x,y,z,w)\in\intz$ whenever $x,y,z,w\in\intz$.
First we will show that it is not possible to parametrize \Pt s 
by a single triple of polynomials with integer coefficients in
any number of variables.

Note, however, that every set of $k$-tuples of integers that is
parametrizable by a single $k$-tuple of integer-valued polynomials 
is parametrizable by a finite number of $k$-tuples of polynomials
with integer coefficients \cite{Fri--RPP}.

\profess{Remark.} 
There do not exist $f,g,h\in \intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ for any $n$
such that $(f,g,h)$ parametrizes the set of \Pt s.
\endprofess

\proof
Suppose $(f,g,h)$ parametrizes the \Pt s. As $\intz[\x]$ is a unique
factorization domain, there exists $d=\gcd(g,h)$ (unique up to sign),
which also divides $f$, since $f^2+g^2=h^2$. 
Let $\varphi=f/d$, $\psi=g/d$ and $\theta=h/d$. 

Then $$\varphi^2= \theta^2 - \psi^2=(\theta+\psi)(\theta-\psi)$$
and $\gcd((\theta+\psi), (\theta-\psi))$ is either $1$ or $2$, but
it can't be $2$, because there exist \Pt s with odd first coordinate
such as $(3,4,5)$. Since $(\theta+\psi)$ and $(\theta-\psi)$ are
co-prime and their product is a square, $(\theta+\psi)$ and
$(\theta-\psi)$ are either both squares, or both $(-1)$ times a square,
and we can get rid of the latter alternative by retro-actively changing
the sign of the polynomial $d$, if necessary.

So there exist polynomials $s$ and $t$ with $(\theta+\psi)=s^2$
and $(\theta-\psi)=t^2$, and therefore 
$$\theta= {s^2+t^2\over 2}\quad \hbox{\rm and}\quad
\psi = {s^2-t^2\over 2}.$$

Since $s^2-t^2 =(s+t)(s-t)$ is divisible by $2$, it is actually 
divisible by $4$, so that $\psi $ is divisible by $2$, which
contradicts the existence of \Pt s with odd second coordinate
such as $(4,3,5)$.
\endproof

%Let $$\Int(\intz^n)=\{f\in\ratq[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\mid
%\forall {\underline a}\in \intz^n\; f({\underline a})\in\intz\},$$
%the ring of integer-valued polynomials in $n$ variables,
%cf. \cite{CaCh97ivp}.
%
In a way, it was the unique factorization property of $\intz[\x]$
that prevented us from finding a triple of polynomials in $\intz[\x]$
parametrizing \Pt s. Before we construct a parametrization
of \Pt s by a triple of integer-valued polynomials, we remark in
passing that $\Int(\intz^n)$ does not enjoy unique factorization
into irreducibles. An example of non-unique factorization into 
irreducibles in $\Int(\intz)$ is given by 
$$x(x-1)\ldots(x-k+1)=k! {x\choose k}.$$
The lefthand side is a product of $k$ irreducibles, while the 
righthand side, after factorization of $k!$ in $\intz$, becomes a
product of far more irreducibles (for large $k$).
(See \cite{CaCh97ivp} for integer-valued polynomials in general,
and \cite{AnCaChSm95FP,CahCha95El,ChaMcC05IPFE} for factorization
properties.)

\profess{Theorem.}
There exist $f,g,h\in \Int(\intz^4)$ such that $(f,g,h)$
parametrizes the set of \Pt s (as the variables range through $\intz$)
namely,
$$\displaylines{
\Biggl( {(2x-xw)((y+zw)^2-(z-yw)^2)\over 2},\hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl)} (2x-xw)(y+zw)(z-yw), \hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl(} {(2x-xw)((y+zw)^2+(z-yw)^2)\over 2}\Biggr).\cr
}$$
\endprofess

\proof
Every \Pt\ $(x,y,z)$ with $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is either of the
form
$$T_1(a,b)=(a^2-b^2,\; 2ab,\; a^2+b^2),$$
or of the form
$$T_2(a,b)=(2ab,\; a^2-b^2,\; a^2+b^2),$$
with $a,b\in \intz$.
Since $$ 2\, T_2(a,b) = T_1(a+b,\> a-b),$$ every \Pt\ with
$\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is of
the form $c\, T_1(a,b)/2$ with $c\in\{1,2\}$ and $a,b\in \intz$.
Let 
$$T(a,b,c)=
\left({c(a^2-b^2)\over 2},\; cab,\; {c(a^2+b^2)\over 2}\right).$$
Then every \Pt\ is of the form $T(a,b,c)$ with 
$a,b,c\in\intz$. Also, every triple $T(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c\in\intz$
is a rational solution of $x^2+y^2=z^2$.

So, the set of \Pt s is precisely the set of integer triples in
the range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$.

Now $T(a,b,c)\in \intz^3$ if and only if $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or
$a\congr b$ mod $2$.
Triples $(a,b,c)\in\intz^3$ satisfying this condition can be 
parametrized by (for instance) 
$$(y+zw,\; z-yw,\; 2x-xw).$$ 
Indeed, if $w$ is even then $c\congr 0$ mod $2$, if $w$ is odd then 
$a\congr b$ mod $2$, and all $(a,b,c)$ satisfying either congruence
actually occur for some $(x,y,z,w)\in\intz^4$, as can be seen by
setting $w=0$ or $w=1$.

Therefore, substituting $y+zw$ for $a$, $z-yw$ for $b$,
and $2x-xw$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ yields a parametrization of
the set of \Pt s by a triple of integer-valued polynomials.
\endproof

\profess{Remark.}
The set of positive \Pt s is parametrized by
$$\displaylines{
\Biggl( {(x+(1-w)^2x)((y+(1+w)z)^2-y^2)\over 2} \vphantom{\Biggr)},\hfill\cr
\hfill\vphantom{\Biggl({1\over f}} (x+(1-w)^2x)(y+(1+w)z)y, \hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl(} {(x+(1-w)^2x)((y+(1+w)z)^2+y^2)\over 2}\Biggr).\cr
}$$
where $x,y,z$ range through the positive integers and $w$ through the
non-negative integers. From this formula, a parametrization of positive
\Pt s with integer parameters can be obtained (using the 4-square theorem)
by replacing $w$ by $w_1^2+w_2^2+w_3^2+w_4^2$ and $x,\,y,\,z$ by
$x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2+x_4^2+1$, $y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2+y_4^2+1$, 
and $z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2+z_4^2+1$, respectively.
\endprofess

\proof
As in the proof of the theorem above, the positive \Pt s are
precisely the triples with positive integer coordinates in the
range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$.
Now $T(a,b,c)$ is a positive triple if and only if $a,b,c$ are
positive integers with $a> b$ and either $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or
$a\congr b$ mod $2$.
Such triples $(a,b,c)$ are parametrized by (for instance)
$$(y+(1+w)z,\> y,\> x+(1-w)^2x)$$
with $x,y,z>0$ and $w\ge 0$. Therefore substituting $y+(1+w)z$ for
$a$, $y$ for $b$ and $x+(1-w)^2x$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ gives a
parametrization of positive \Pt s where $w$ ranges through 
non-negative integers and $x,y,z$ through positive integers.
The 4-square theorem allows us to convert this to a parametrization
with 16 integer parameters.
\endproof

```lean
import Mathlib

open scoped BigOperators

/-! # Parametrization of Pythagorean Triples by Polynomials

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

end Definitions

section Constructions

/-- The first component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def f_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w
  (c * (u^2 - v^2)) / 2

/-- The second component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def g_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w
  c * u * v

/-- The third component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def h_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w
  (c * (u^2 + v^2)) / 2

/-- The explicit parametrization as a triple (Theorem, line 194). -/
def T_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ × ℤ × ℤ := (f_param a, g_param a, h_param a)

/-- The first component of the positive triples parametrization (Remark, line 240). -/
def f_pos_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := x + (1 - w)^2 * x
  let u := y + (1 + w) * z
  (c * (u^2 - y^2)) / 2

/-- The second component of the positive triples parametrization (Remark, line 240). -/
def g_pos_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := x + (1 - w)^2 * x
  let u := y + (1 + w) * z
  c * u * y

/-- The third component of the positive triples parametrization (Remark, line 240). -/

  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := x + (1 - w)^2 * x
  let u := y + (1 + w) * z
  (c * (u^2 + y^2)) / 2

/-- The positive triples parametrization as a triple (Remark, line 240). -/
def T_pos_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ × ℤ × ℤ := (f_pos_param a, g_pos_param a, h_pos_param a)

section Theorems

/-!
### Remark (line 143): Impossibility with integer coefficient polynomials

**Source proof:** Suppose (f,g,h) parametrizes the PTs. As ℤ[x] is a UFD,
there exists d = gcd(g,h) which also divides f since f²+g²=h². Let φ=f/d,
ψ=g/d, θ=h/d. Then φ² = (θ+ψ)(θ-ψ). The gcd of (θ+ψ) and (θ-ψ) is either 1
or 2, but not 2 because there exist PTs with odd first coordinate. Since they
are coprime and their product is a square, each is a square (up to sign).
Changing the sign of d if needed, we get θ+ψ = s² and θ-ψ = t². Then
θ = (s²+t²)/2 and ψ = (s²-t²)/2. Since s²-t² is divisible by 4, ψ is
divisible by 2, contradicting the existence of PTs with odd second coordinate.
-/

/-- There do not exist polynomials f,g,h ∈ ℤ[x₁,...,xₙ] for any n that parametrize
all Pythagorean triples. -/
theorem no_integer_poly_parametrization :
    ¬∃ (n : ℕ) (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ),
      IsPolyParametrization pythagoreanTriples f g h := by
  sorry

/-!
### Theorem (line 194): Existence with integer-valued polynomials

**Source proof:** Every primitive PT is T₁(a,b) or T₂(a,b). Since
2·T₂(a,b) = T₁(a+b,a-b), every primitive PT is c·T₁(a,b)/2 with c∈{1,2}.
Define T(a,b,c) = (c(a²-b²)/2, cab, c(a²+b²)/2). Every PT is T(a,b,c) for
some a,b,c ∈ ℤ. Also T(a,b,c) ∈ ℤ³ iff c ≡ 0 (mod 2) or a ≡ b (mod 2).
Triples satisfying this are parametrized by (y+zw, z-yw, 2x-xw). Substituting
gives the explicit parametrization.
-/

/-- The rational parametrization T(a,b,c) = (c(a²-b²)/2, cab, c(a²+b²)/2). -/
def T_abc (a b c : ℤ) : ℚ × ℚ × ℚ :=
  (c * (a^2 - b^2) / 2, c * a * b, c * (a^2 + b^2) / 2)

/-- Every Pythagorean triple is of the form T(a,b,c) for integers a,b,c. -/
lemma all_pts_from_T (x y z : ℤ) (h : x^2 + y^2 = z^2) :
    ∃ a b c : ℤ, (x, y, z) = T_abc a b c := by
  sorry

/-- T(a,b,c) has integer coordinates iff c is even or a ≡ b (mod 2). -/
lemma T_integer_condition (a b c : ℤ) :
    (∃ x y z : ℤ, (x, y, z) = T_abc a b c) ↔ (Even c ∨ a ≡ b [ZMOD 2]) := by
  sorry

/-- The condition "c even or a ≡ b (mod 2)" is parametrized by (y+zw, z-yw, 2x-xw). -/
lemma condition_parametrization :
    {(a, b, c) : ℤ × ℤ × ℤ | Even c ∨ a ≡ b [ZMOD 2]} =
    (fun (p : Fin 4 → ℤ) => (p 1 + p 2 * p 3, p 2 - p 1 * p 3, 2 * p 0 - p 0 * p 3)) '' Set.univ := by
  sorry

/-- There exists a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables that
parametrizes all Pythagorean triples. -/
theorem exists_int_valued_parametrization :
    IsParametrization pythagoreanTriples T_param := by
  sorry

/-!
### Remark (line 240): Positive Pythagorean triples parametrization

**Source proof:** Positive PTs are T(a,b,c) with a,b,c > 0, a > b, and
either c even or a ≡ b (mod 2). Such triples are parametrized by
(y+(1+w)z, y, x+(1-w)²x) with x,y,z > 0 and w ≥ 0. Substituting gives
the explicit parametrization.
-/

/-- The domain for positive triples parametrization. -/
def positiveDomain : Set (Fin 4 → ℤ) :=
  {a | 0 < a 0 ∧ 0 < a 1 ∧ 0 < a 2 ∧ 0 ≤ a 3}

/-- Positive Pythagorean triples are parametrized by T_pos_param on the
positive domain. -/
theorem positive_triples_parametrization :
    IsParametrizationOn positivePythagoreanTriples positiveDomain T_pos_param := by
  sorry

end Theorems

open scoped BigOperators

/-! # Parametrization of Pythagorean Triples by Polynomials

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

end Definitions

section Constructions

  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w

/-- The second component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/

  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w

/-- The third component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def h_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=

  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w

This gives T(a,b,c). -/

/-!
### Remark (line 143): Impossibility with integer coefficient polynomials

**Source proof:** Suppose (f,g,h) parametrizes the PTs. As ℤ[x] is a UFD,

ψ=g/d, θ=h/d. Then φ² = (θ+ψ)(θ-ψ). The gcd of (θ+ψ) and (θ-ψ) is either 1

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

end Definitions

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer

- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued

- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/]

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- A function f : (Fin n → ℤ) → ℤ is an integer-valued polynomial if it is
    the evaluation of a rational polynomial at integer points. -/
def IsIntValuedPoly {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℤ) → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∃ p : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ, ∀ a, f a = MvPolynomial.eval (fun i => (a i : ℚ)) p

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/

    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a =>
    (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

/-! # Parametrization of Pythagorean Triples by Polynomials

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- A function f : (Fin n → ℤ) → ℤ is an integer-valued polynomial if it is
    the evaluation of a rational polynomial at integer points. -/
def IsIntValuedPoly {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℤ) → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∃ p : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ, ∀ a, f a = MvPolynomial.eval (fun i => (a i : ℚ)) p

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=

\bigskip\bigskip\medskip
 

{\bf Abstract.} 
It is well known that Pythagorean triples can be parametrized by two
triples of polynomials with integer coefficients. We show that no
single triple of polynomials with integer coefficients in any number
of variables is sufficient, but that there exists a parametrization 
of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of integer-valued polynomials.
%MSC 2000: primary 11D09, secondary 11C08, 13F20.
\bigskip\medskip

The second author has recently studied polynomial parametrizations
of solutions of Diophantine equations \cite{Vas--PPDE}, and the 
first author has wondered if it were possible in some cases to
parametrize by a $k$-tuple of integer-valued polynomials a 
solution set that is not parametrizable by a $k$-tuple of 
polynomials with integer coefficients \cite{Fri--RPP}.
\Pt s provide an example that this is indeed so.

We call a triple of integers $(x,y,z)\in\intz^3$ satisfying
$$ x^2+y^2=z^2$$
a \Pt, and, if $x,y,z>0$, a positive \Pt.
%If in addition $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$, we say that $(x,y,z)$ is a primitive \Pt.

It is well known that every \Pt\ is either of the form 
$$\left(c(a^2-b^2),\; 2cab,\; c(a^2+b^2)\right)$$
or of the form
$$\left(2cab,\; c(a^2-b^2),\; c(a^2+b^2)\right)$$
with $a,b,c\in\intz$, see for instance~\cite{HlaSch79ZT}.

To make precise our usage of the term polynomial parametrization,
consider a set $S\subseteq \intz^k$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ be a $k$-tuple
of polynomials either in the ring of polynomials with integer 
coefficients in $n$ variables, $\intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, or in
$$\Int(\intz^n)=\{f\in\ratq[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\mid
\forall a\in \intz^n\; f(a)\in\intz\},$$
the ring of integer-valued polynomials in $n$ variables,
% cf. \cite{CaCh97ivp}, 
for some $n$. In either case $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$
defines a function $F\colon \intz^n\rightarrow \intz^k$.
If $S$ is the image of this function, $S=F(\intz^n)$,
we say that $(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$ parametrizes $S$. We call this a 
parametrization of $S$ by a single $k$-tuple of polynomials.

If $S\subseteq \intz^k$ is the union of the images of finitely many
$k$-tuples of polynomials $F_i=(f_{i1},\ldots,f_{ik})$, 
$S=\bigcup_{i=1}^m F_i(\intz^n)$, we call this a parametrization
of $S$ by a finite number of $k$-tuples of polynomials, and we
distinguish between parametrizations by polynomials with integer
coefficients, meaning $F_i\in (\intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n])^k$ for
all $i$, and by integer-valued polynomials, meaning 
$F_i\in (\Int(\intz^n))^k$.
Unless explicitly specified otherwise, we are using integer parameters,
that is, we let all variables of all polynomials range through the
integers.

We will give a parametrization of the set of \Pt s by a single
triple of integer-valued polynomials in $4$ variables, that is, by 
$(f_1,f_2,f_3)$ with $f_i\in \ratq[x,y,z,w]$ such that
$f_i(x,y,z,w)\in\intz$ whenever $x,y,z,w\in\intz$.
First we will show that it is not possible to parametrize \Pt s 
by a single triple of polynomials with integer coefficients in
any number of variables.

Note, however, that every set of $k$-tuples of integers that is
parametrizable by a single $k$-tuple of integer-valued polynomials 
is parametrizable by a finite number of $k$-tuples of polynomials
with integer coefficients \cite{Fri--RPP}.

\profess{Remark.} 
There do not exist $f,g,h\in \intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ for any $n$
such that $(f,g,h)$ parametrizes the set of \Pt s.
\endprofess

\proof
Suppose $(f,g,h)$ parametrizes the \Pt s. As $\intz[\x]$ is a unique
factorization domain, there exists $d=\gcd(g,h)$ (unique up to sign),
which also divides $f$, since $f^2+g^2=h^2$. 
Let $\varphi=f/d$, $\psi=g/d$ and $\theta=h/d$. 

Then $$\varphi^2= \theta^2 - \psi^2=(\theta+\psi)(\theta-\psi)$$
and $\gcd((\theta+\psi), (\theta-\psi))$ is either $1$ or $2$, but
it can't be $2$, because there exist \Pt s with odd first coordinate
such as $(3,4,5)$. Since $(\theta+\psi)$ and $(\theta-\psi)$ are
co-prime and their product is a square, $(\theta+\psi)$ and
$(\theta-\psi)$ are either both squares, or both $(-1)$ times a square,
and we can get rid of the latter alternative by retro-actively changing
the sign of the polynomial $d$, if necessary.

So there exist polynomials $s$ and $t$ with $(\theta+\psi)=s^2$
and $(\theta-\psi)=t^2$, and therefore 
$$\theta= {s^2+t^2\over 2}\quad \hbox{\rm and}\quad
\psi = {s^2-t^2\over 2}.$$

Since $s^2-t^2 =(s+t)(s-t)$ is divisible by $2$, it is actually 
divisible by $4$, so that $\psi $ is divisible by $2$, which
contradicts the existence of \Pt s with odd second coordinate
such as $(4,3,5)$.
\endproof

%\forall {\underline a}\in \intz^n\; f({\underline a})\in\intz\},$$
%the ring of integer-valued polynomials in $n$ variables,
%cf. \cite{CaCh97ivp}.
%
In a way, it was the unique factorization property of $\intz[\x]$
that prevented us from finding a triple of polynomials in $\intz[\x]$
parametrizing \Pt s. Before we construct a parametrization
of \Pt s by a triple of integer-valued polynomials, we remark in
passing that $\Int(\intz^n)$ does not enjoy unique factorization
into irreducibles. An example of non-unique factorization into 
irreducibles in $\Int(\intz)$ is given by 
$$x(x-1)\ldots(x-k+1)=k! {x\choose k}.$$
The lefthand side is a product of $k$ irreducibles, while the 
righthand side, after factorization of $k!$ in $\intz$, becomes a
product of far more irreducibles (for large $k$).
(See \cite{CaCh97ivp} for integer-valued polynomials in general,
and \cite{AnCaChSm95FP,CahCha95El,ChaMcC05IPFE} for factorization
properties.)

\profess{Theorem.}
There exist $f,g,h\in \Int(\intz^4)$ such that $(f,g,h)$
parametrizes the set of \Pt s (as the variables range through $\intz$)
namely,
$$\displaylines{
\Biggl( {(2x-xw)((y+zw)^2-(z-yw)^2)\over 2},\hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl)} (2x-xw)(y+zw)(z-yw), \hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl(} {(2x-xw)((y+zw)^2+(z-yw)^2)\over 2}\Biggr).\cr
}$$
\endprofess

\proof
Every \Pt\ $(x,y,z)$ with $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is either of the
form
$$T_1(a,b)=(a^2-b^2,\; 2ab,\; a^2+b^2),$$
or of the form
$$T_2(a,b)=(2ab,\; a^2-b^2,\; a^2+b^2),$$
with $a,b\in \intz$.
Since $$ 2\, T_2(a,b) = T_1(a+b,\> a-b),$$ every \Pt\ with
$\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is of
the form $c\, T_1(a,b)/2$ with $c\in\{1,2\}$ and $a,b\in \intz$.
Let 
$$T(a,b,c)=
\left({c(a^2-b^2)\over 2},\; cab,\; {c(a^2+b^2)\over 2}\right).$$
Then every \Pt\ is of the form $T(a,b,c)$ with 
$a,b,c\in\intz$. Also, every triple $T(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c\in\intz$
is a rational solution of $x^2+y^2=z^2$.

So, the set of \Pt s is precisely the set of integer triples in
the range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$.

Now $T(a,b,c)\in \intz^3$ if and only if $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or
$a\congr b$ mod $2$.
Triples $(a,b,c)\in\intz^3$ satisfying this condition can be 
parametrized by (for instance) 
$$(y+zw,\; z-yw,\; 2x-xw).$$ 
Indeed, if $w$ is even then $c\congr 0$ mod $2$, if $w$ is odd then 
$a\congr b$ mod $2$, and all $(a,b,c)$ satisfying either congruence
actually occur for some $(x,y,z,w)\in\intz^4$, as can be seen by
setting $w=0$ or $w=1$.

Therefore, substituting $y+zw$ for $a$, $z-yw$ for $b$,
and $2x-xw$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ yields a parametrization of
the set of \Pt s by a triple of integer-valued polynomials.
\endproof

\profess{Remark.}
The set of positive \Pt s is parametrized by
$$\displaylines{
\Biggl( {(x+(1-w)^2x)((y+(1+w)z)^2-y^2)\over 2} \vphantom{\Biggr)},\hfill\cr
\hfill\vphantom{\Biggl({1\over f}} (x+(1-w)^2x)(y+(1+w)z)y, \hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl(} {(x+(1-w)^2x)((y+(1+w)z)^2+y^2)\over 2}\Biggr).\cr
}$$
where $x,y,z$ range through the positive integers and $w$ through the
non-negative integers. From this formula, a parametrization of positive
\Pt s with integer parameters can be obtained (using the 4-square theorem)
by replacing $w$ by $w_1^2+w_2^2+w_3^2+w_4^2$ and $x,\,y,\,z$ by
$x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2+x_4^2+1$, $y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2+y_4^2+1$, 
and $z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2+z_4^2+1$, respectively.
\endprofess

\proof
As in the proof of the theorem above, the positive \Pt s are
precisely the triples with positive integer coordinates in the
range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$.
Now $T(a,b,c)$ is a positive triple if and only if $a,b,c$ are
positive integers with $a> b$ and either $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or
$a\congr b$ mod $2$.
Such triples $(a,b,c)$ are parametrized by (for instance)
$$(y+(1+w)z,\> y,\> x+(1-w)^2x)$$
with $x,y,z>0$ and $w\ge 0$. Therefore substituting $y+(1+w)z$ for
$a$, $y$ for $b$ and $x+(1-w)^2x$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ gives a
parametrization of positive \Pt s where $w$ ranges through 
non-negative integers and $x,y,z$ through positive integers.
The 4-square theorem allows us to convert this to a parametrization
with 16 integer parameters.
\endproof

```lean
import Mathlib

open scoped BigOperators

/-! # Parametrization of Pythagorean Triples by Polynomials

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

end Definitions

section Constructions

/-- The first component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def f_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w

/-- The second component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def g_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w
  c * u * v

/-- The third component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/
def h_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w
  (c * (u^2 + v^2)) / 2

/-- The explicit parametrization as a triple (Theorem, line 194). -/
def T_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ × ℤ × ℤ := (f_param a, g_param a, h_param a)

/-- The first component of the positive triples parametrization (Remark, line 240). -/
def f_pos_param (a : Fin 4 → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  let x := a 0
  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := x + (1 - w)^2 * x
  let u := y + (1 + w) * z

section Theorems

/-!
### Remark (line 143): Impossibility with integer coefficient polynomials

**Source proof:** Suppose (f,g,h) parametrizes the PTs. As ℤ[x] is a UFD,
there exists d = gcd(g,h) which also divides f since f²+g²=h². Let φ=f/d,
ψ=g/d, θ=h/d. Then φ² = (θ+ψ)(θ-ψ). The gcd of (θ+ψ) and (θ-ψ) is either 1
or 2, but not 2 because there exist PTs with odd first coordinate. Since they
are coprime and their product is a square, each is a square (up to sign).
Changing the sign of d if needed, we get θ+ψ = s² and θ-ψ = t². Then
θ = (s²+t²)/2 and ψ = (s²-t²)/2. Since s²-t² is divisible by 4, ψ is
divisible by 2, contradicting the existence of PTs with odd second coordinate.
-/

/-- There do not exist polynomials f,g,h ∈ ℤ[x₁,...,xₙ] for any n that parametrize
all Pythagorean triples. -/
theorem no_integer_poly_parametrization :
    ¬∃ (n : ℕ) (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ),
      IsPolyParametrization pythagoreanTriples f g h := by
  sorry

/-!
### Theorem (line 194): Existence with integer-valued polynomials

**Source proof:** Every primitive PT is T₁(a,b) or T₂(a,b). Since
2·T₂(a,b) = T₁(a+b,a-b), every primitive PT is c·T₁(a,b)/2 with c∈{1,2}.
Define T(a,b,c) = (c(a²-b²)/2, cab, c(a²+b²)/2). Every PT is T(a,b,c) for
some a,b,c ∈ ℤ. Also T(a,b,c) ∈ ℤ³ iff c ≡ 0 (mod 2) or a ≡ b (mod 2).
Triples satisfying this are parametrized by (y+zw, z-yw, 2x-xw). Substituting
gives the explicit parametrization.
-/

/-- The rational parametrization T(a,b,c) = (c(a²-b²)/2, cab, c(a²+b²)/2). -/
def T_abc (a b c : ℤ) : ℚ × ℚ × ℚ :=
  (c * (a^2 - b^2) / 2, c * a * b, c * (a^2 + b^2) / 2)

/-- Every Pythagorean triple is of the form T(a,b,c) for integers a,b,c. -/
lemma all_pts_from_T (x y z : ℤ) (h : x^2 + y^2 = z^2) :
    ∃ a b c : ℤ, (x, y, z) = T_abc a b c := by
  sorry

/-- T(a,b,c) has integer coordinates iff c is even or a ≡ b (mod 2). -/
lemma T_integer_condition (a b c : ℤ) :
    (∃ x y z : ℤ, (x, y, z) = T_abc a b c) ↔ (Even c ∨ a ≡ b [ZMOD 2]) := by
  sorry

/-- The condition "c even or a ≡ b (mod 2)" is parametrized by (y+zw, z-yw, 2x-xw). -/
lemma condition_parametrization :
    {(a, b, c) : ℤ × ℤ × ℤ | Even c ∨ a ≡ b [ZMOD 2]} =
    (fun (p : Fin 4 → ℤ) => (p 1 + p 2 * p 3, p 2 - p 1 * p 3, 2 * p 0 - p 0 * p 3)) '' Set.univ := by
  sorry

/-- There exists a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables that
parametrizes all Pythagorean triples. -/
theorem exists_int_valued_parametrization :
    IsParametrization pythagoreanTriples T_param := by
  sorry

/-!
### Remark (line 240): Positive Pythagorean triples parametrization

**Source proof:** Positive PTs are T(a,b,c) with a,b,c > 0, a > b, and
either c even or a ≡ b (mod 2). Such triples are parametrized by
(y+(1+w)z, y, x+(1-w)²x) with x,y,z > 0 and w ≥ 0. Substituting gives
the explicit parametrization.
-/

/-- The domain for positive triples parametrization. -/
def positiveDomain : Set (Fin 4 → ℤ) :=
  {a | 0 < a 0 ∧ 0 < a 1 ∧ 0 < a 2 ∧ 0 ≤ a 3}

/-- Positive Pythagorean triples are parametrized by T_pos_param on the
positive domain. -/
theorem positive_triples_parametrization :
    IsParametrizationOn positivePythagoreanTriples positiveDomain T_pos_param := by
  sorry

end Theorems

/-! # Parametrization of Pythagorean Triples by Polynomials

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

end Definitions

  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w

/-- The second component of the explicit parametrization (Theorem, line 194). -/

  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w

  let y := a 1
  let z := a 2
  let w := a 3
  let c := 2 * x - x * w
  let u := y + z * w
  let v := z - y * w

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a => (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

end Definitions

-/]

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x^2 + y^2 = z^2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=

This file formalizes results from Frisch and Vaserstein's paper
"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- A function f : (Fin n → ℤ) → ℤ is an integer-valued polynomial if it is
    the evaluation of a rational polynomial at integer points. -/
def IsIntValuedPoly {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℤ) → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∃ p : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ, ∀ a, f a = MvPolynomial.eval (fun i => (a i : ℚ)) p

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (f g h : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ) : Prop :=
  IsParametrization S (fun a =>
    (MvPolynomial.eval a f, MvPolynomial.eval a g, MvPolynomial.eval a h))

/-! # Parametrization of Pythagorean Triples by Polynomials

"Parametrization of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of polynomials".

## Main results

- `no_integer_poly_parametrization`: No triple of polynomials with integer
  coefficients in any number of variables parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `exists_int_valued_parametrization`: There exists a triple of integer-valued
  polynomials in 4 variables that parametrizes all Pythagorean triples.
- `positive_triples_parametrization`: The set of positive Pythagorean triples
  is parametrized by a triple of integer-valued polynomials in 4 variables
  (with restricted domain).
-/

section Definitions

/-- The set of all Pythagorean triples. -/
def pythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- The set of positive Pythagorean triples. -/
def positivePythagoreanTriples : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {(x, y, z) | 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧ x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 = z ^ 2}

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized by a function F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = range(F). -/
def IsParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = Set.range F

/-- A set S ⊆ ℤ³ is parametrized on a domain D ⊆ ℤⁿ by F : ℤⁿ → ℤ³ if S = F(D). -/
def IsParametrizationOn (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}
    (D : Set (Fin n → ℤ)) (F : (Fin n → ℤ) → (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  S = F '' D

/-- A function f : (Fin n → ℤ) → ℤ is an integer-valued polynomial if it is
    the evaluation of a rational polynomial at integer points. -/
def IsIntValuedPoly {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℤ) → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∃ p : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ, ∀ a, f a = MvPolynomial.eval (fun i => (a i : ℚ)) p

/-- Parametrization by integer coefficient polynomials. -/
def IsPolyParametrization (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) {n : ℕ}

   Source proof excerpt: Every \Pt\ $(x,y,z)$ with $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is either of the form $$T_1(a,b)=(a^2-b^2,\; 2ab,\; a^2+b^2),$$ or of the form $$T_2(a,b)=(2ab,\; a^2-b^2,\; a^2+b^2),$$ with $a,b\in \intz$. Since $$ 2\, T_2(a,b) = T_1(a+b,\> a-b),$$ every \Pt\ with $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is of the form $c\, T_1(a,b)/2$ with $c\in\{1,2\}$ and $a,b\in \intz$. Let $$T(a,b,c)= \left({c(a^2-b^2)\over 2},\; cab,\; {c(a^2+b^2)\over 2}\right).$$ Then every \Pt\ is of the form $T(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c\in\intz$. Also, every triple $T(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c\in\intz$ is a rational solution of $x^2+y^2=z^2$. So, the set of \Pt s is precisely the set of integer triples in the range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$. Now $T(a,b,c)\in \intz^3$ if and only if $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or $a\congr b$ mod $2$. Triples $(a,b,c)\in\intz^3$ satisfying this condition can be parametrized by (for instance) $$(y+zw,\; z-yw,\; 2x-xw).$$ Indeed, if $w$ is even then $c\congr 0$ mod $2$, if $w$ is odd then $a\congr b$ mod $2$, and all $(a,b,c)$ satisfying either congruence actually occur for some $(x,y,z,w)\in\intz^4$, as can be seen by setting $w=0$ or $w=1$. Therefore, substituting $y+zw$ for $a$, $z-yw$ for $b$, and $2x-xw$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ yields a parametrization of the set of \Pt s by a triple of integer-valued polynomials.
   Source proof locator: lines 203-238
3. `line-240` (remark, lines 240-253) - Remark.

From this formula, a parametrization of positive \Pt s with integer parameters can be obtained (using the 4-square theorem) by replacing $w$ by $w_1^2+w_2^2+w_3^2+w_4^2$ and $x,\,y,\,z$ by $x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2+x_4^2+1$, $y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2+y_4^2+1$, and $z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2+z_4^2+1$, respectively.
   Source proof excerpt: As in the proof of the theorem above, the positive \Pt s are precisely the triples with positive integer coordinates in the range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$. Now $T(a,b,c)$ is a positive triple if and only if $a,b,c$ are positive integers with $a> b$ and either $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or $a\congr b$ mod $2$. Such triples $(a,b,c)$ are parametrized by (for instance) $$(y+(1+w)z,\> y,\> x+(1-w)^2x)$$ with $x,y,z>0$ and $w\ge 0$. Therefore substituting $y+(1+w)z$ for $a$, $y$ for $b$ and $x+(1-w)^2x$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ gives a parametrization of positive \Pt s where $w$ ranges through non-negative integers and $x,y,z$ through positive integers. The 4-square theorem allows us to convert this to a parametrization with 16 integer parameters.
   Source proof locator: lines 253-270

\centerline{\titlefont Parametrization of Pythagorean triples}
\smallskip
\centerline{\titlefont by a single triple of polynomials}
\bigskip\medskip

\centerline{\authorfont Sophie Frisch {\tenrm and} Leonid Vaserstein}
\footnote{\vphantom{*}}
{2000 Math.~Subj.~Classification: primary 11D09, secondary 11D85, 11C08, 13F20.}
\bigskip\bigskip\medskip
 

{\bf Abstract.} 
It is well known that Pythagorean triples can be parametrized by two
triples of polynomials with integer coefficients. We show that no
single triple of polynomials with integer coefficients in any number
of variables is sufficient, but that there exists a parametrization 
of Pythagorean triples by a single triple of integer-valued polynomials.
%MSC 2000: primary 11D09, secondary 11C08, 13F20.
\bigskip\medskip

The second author has recently studied polynomial parametrizations
of solutions of Diophantine equations \cite{Vas--PPDE}, and the 
first author has wondered if it were possible in some cases to
parametrize by a $k$-tuple of integer-valued polynomials a 
solution set that is not parametrizable by a $k$-tuple of 
polynomials with integer coefficients \cite{Fri--RPP}.
\Pt s provide an example that this is indeed so.

We call a triple of integers $(x,y,z)\in\intz^3$ satisfying
$$ x^2+y^2=z^2$$
a \Pt, and, if $x,y,z>0$, a positive \Pt.
%If in addition $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$, we say that $(x,y,z)$ is a primitive \Pt.

It is well known that every \Pt\ is either of the form 
$$\left(c(a^2-b^2),\; 2cab,\; c(a^2+b^2)\right)$$
or of the form
$$\left(2cab,\; c(a^2-b^2),\; c(a^2+b^2)\right)$$
with $a,b,c\in\intz$, see for instance~\cite{HlaSch79ZT}.

To make precise our usage of the term polynomial parametrization,
consider a set $S\subseteq \intz^k$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ be a $k$-tuple
of polynomials either in the ring of polynomials with integer 
coefficients in $n$ variables, $\intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, or in
$$\Int(\intz^n)=\{f\in\ratq[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\mid
\forall a\in \intz^n\; f(a)\in\intz\},$$
the ring of integer-valued polynomials in $n$ variables,
% cf. \cite{CaCh97ivp}, 
for some $n$. In either case $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$
defines a function $F\colon \intz^n\rightarrow \intz^k$.
If $S$ is the image of this function, $S=F(\intz^n)$,
we say that $(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$ parametrizes $S$. We call this a 
parametrization of $S$ by a single $k$-tuple of polynomials.

If $S\subseteq \intz^k$ is the union of the images of finitely many
$k$-tuples of polynomials $F_i=(f_{i1},\ldots,f_{ik})$, 
$S=\bigcup_{i=1}^m F_i(\intz^n)$, we call this a parametrization
of $S$ by a finite number of $k$-tuples of polynomials, and we
distinguish between parametrizations by polynomials with integer
coefficients, meaning $F_i\in (\intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n])^k$ for
all $i$, and by integer-valued polynomials, meaning 
$F_i\in (\Int(\intz^n))^k$.
Unless explicitly specified otherwise, we are using integer parameters,
that is, we let all variables of all polynomials range through the
integers.

We will give a parametrization of the set of \Pt s by a single
triple of integer-valued polynomials in $4$ variables, that is, by 
$(f_1,f_2,f_3)$ with $f_i\in \ratq[x,y,z,w]$ such that
$f_i(x,y,z,w)\in\intz$ whenever $x,y,z,w\in\intz$.
First we will show that it is not possible to parametrize \Pt s 
by a single triple of polynomials with integer coefficients in
any number of variables.

Note, however, that every set of $k$-tuples of integers that is
parametrizable by a single $k$-tuple of integer-valued polynomials 
is parametrizable by a finite number of $k$-tuples of polynomials
with integer coefficients \cite{Fri--RPP}.

\profess{Remark.} 
There do not exist $f,g,h\in \intz[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ for any $n$
such that $(f,g,h)$ parametrizes the set of \Pt s.
\endprofess

\proof
Suppose $(f,g,h)$ parametrizes the \Pt s. As $\intz[\x]$ is a unique
factorization domain, there exists $d=\gcd(g,h)$ (unique up to sign),
which also divides $f$, since $f^2+g^2=h^2$. 
Let $\varphi=f/d$, $\psi=g/d$ and $\theta=h/d$. 

Then $$\varphi^2= \theta^2 - \psi^2=(\theta+\psi)(\theta-\psi)$$
and $\gcd((\theta+\psi), (\theta-\psi))$ is either $1$ or $2$, but
it can't be $2$, because there exist \Pt s with odd first coordinate
such as $(3,4,5)$. Since $(\theta+\psi)$ and $(\theta-\psi)$ are
co-prime and their product is a square, $(\theta+\psi)$ and
$(\theta-\psi)$ are either both squares, or both $(-1)$ times a square,
and we can get rid of the latter alternative by retro-actively changing
the sign of the polynomial $d$, if necessary.

So there exist polynomials $s$ and $t$ with $(\theta+\psi)=s^2$
and $(\theta-\psi)=t^2$, and therefore 
$$\theta= {s^2+t^2\over 2}\quad \hbox{\rm and}\quad
\psi = {s^2-t^2\over 2}.$$

Since $s^2-t^2 =(s+t)(s-t)$ is divisible by $2$, it is actually 
divisible by $4$, so that $\psi $ is divisible by $2$, which
contradicts the existence of \Pt s with odd second coordinate
such as $(4,3,5)$.
\endproof

%Let $$\Int(\intz^n)=\{f\in\ratq[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\mid
%\forall {\underline a}\in \intz^n\; f({\underline a})\in\intz\},$$
%the ring of integer-valued polynomials in $n$ variables,
%cf. \cite{CaCh97ivp}.
%
In a way, it was the unique factorization property of $\intz[\x]$
that prevented us from finding a triple of polynomials in $\intz[\x]$
parametrizing \Pt s. Before we construct a parametrization
of \Pt s by a triple of integer-valued polynomials, we remark in
passing that $\Int(\intz^n)$ does not enjoy unique factorization
into irreducibles. An example of non-unique factorization into 
irreducibles in $\Int(\intz)$ is given by 
$$x(x-1)\ldots(x-k+1)=k! {x\choose k}.$$
The lefthand side is a product of $k$ irreducibles, while the 
righthand side, after factorization of $k!$ in $\intz$, becomes a
product of far more irreducibles (for large $k$).
(See \cite{CaCh97ivp} for integer-valued polynomials in general,
and \cite{AnCaChSm95FP,CahCha95El,ChaMcC05IPFE} for factorization
properties.)

\profess{Theorem.}
There exist $f,g,h\in \Int(\intz^4)$ such that $(f,g,h)$
parametrizes the set of \Pt s (as the variables range through $\intz$)
namely,
$$\displaylines{
\Biggl( {(2x-xw)((y+zw)^2-(z-yw)^2)\over 2},\hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl)} (2x-xw)(y+zw)(z-yw), \hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl(} {(2x-xw)((y+zw)^2+(z-yw)^2)\over 2}\Biggr).\cr
}$$
\endprofess

\proof
Every \Pt\ $(x,y,z)$ with $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is either of the
form
$$T_1(a,b)=(a^2-b^2,\; 2ab,\; a^2+b^2),$$
or of the form
$$T_2(a,b)=(2ab,\; a^2-b^2,\; a^2+b^2),$$
with $a,b\in \intz$.
Since $$ 2\, T_2(a,b) = T_1(a+b,\> a-b),$$ every \Pt\ with
$\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $z>0$ is of
the form $c\, T_1(a,b)/2$ with $c\in\{1,2\}$ and $a,b\in \intz$.
Let 
$$T(a,b,c)=
\left({c(a^2-b^2)\over 2},\; cab,\; {c(a^2+b^2)\over 2}\right).$$
Then every \Pt\ is of the form $T(a,b,c)$ with 
$a,b,c\in\intz$. Also, every triple $T(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c\in\intz$
is a rational solution of $x^2+y^2=z^2$.

So, the set of \Pt s is precisely the set of integer triples in
the range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$.

Now $T(a,b,c)\in \intz^3$ if and only if $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or
$a\congr b$ mod $2$.
Triples $(a,b,c)\in\intz^3$ satisfying this condition can be 
parametrized by (for instance) 
$$(y+zw,\; z-yw,\; 2x-xw).$$ 
Indeed, if $w$ is even then $c\congr 0$ mod $2$, if $w$ is odd then 
$a\congr b$ mod $2$, and all $(a,b,c)$ satisfying either congruence
actually occur for some $(x,y,z,w)\in\intz^4$, as can be seen by
setting $w=0$ or $w=1$.

Therefore, substituting $y+zw$ for $a$, $z-yw$ for $b$,
and $2x-xw$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ yields a parametrization of
the set of \Pt s by a triple of integer-valued polynomials.
\endproof

\profess{Remark.}
The set of positive \Pt s is parametrized by
$$\displaylines{
\Biggl( {(x+(1-w)^2x)((y+(1+w)z)^2-y^2)\over 2} \vphantom{\Biggr)},\hfill\cr
\hfill\vphantom{\Biggl({1\over f}} (x+(1-w)^2x)(y+(1+w)z)y, \hfill\cr
\hfill \vphantom{\Biggl(} {(x+(1-w)^2x)((y+(1+w)z)^2+y^2)\over 2}\Biggr).\cr
}$$
where $x,y,z$ range through the positive integers and $w$ through the
non-negative integers. From this formula, a parametrization of positive
\Pt s with integer parameters can be obtained (using the 4-square theorem)
by replacing $w$ by $w_1^2+w_2^2+w_3^2+w_4^2$ and $x,\,y,\,z$ by
$x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2+x_4^2+1$, $y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2+y_4^2+1$, 
and $z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2+z_4^2+1$, respectively.
\endprofess

\proof
As in the proof of the theorem above, the positive \Pt s are
precisely the triples with positive integer coordinates in the
range of the function $T\colon \intz^3\rightarrow \ratq^3$.
Now $T(a,b,c)$ is a positive triple if and only if $a,b,c$ are
positive integers with $a> b$ and either $c\congr 0$ mod $2$ or
$a\congr b$ mod $2$.
Such triples $(a,b,c)$ are parametrized by (for instance)
$$(y+(1+w)z,\> y,\> x+(1-w)^2x)$$
with $x,y,z>0$ and $w\ge 0$. Therefore substituting $y+(1+w)z$ for
$a$, $y$ for $b$ and $x+(1-w)^2x$ for $c$ in $T(a,b,c)$ gives a
parametrization of positive \Pt s where $w$ ranges through 
non-negative integers and $x,y,z$ through positive integers.
The 4-square theorem allows us to convert this to a parametrization
with 16 integer parameters.
\endproof
